spans.assertion: the analysis used data from soccer leagues in England, Germany, France and Spain for the 2012-2013 season, a dataset of 146,028 player-referee dyads, to examine whether referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players
115,603 of the 146,028 dyads (79.2%) were retained for a complete-case analysis after excluding dyads with missing skin tone ratings or missing covariates
the adjusted risk difference shows dark-skinned players have a 0.184 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card than light-skinned players (95% CI [0.012,0.355], p=0.035)
the adjusted odds ratio for red card given dark vs light skin is 1.157 (95% CI [1.016,1.318], p=0.028), i.e. 15.7% higher odds
the hypothesis is concluded to be SUPPORTED by statistically significant evidence at α=0.05

the 95% CI for the adjusted risk difference excludes zero, taken as evidence dark-skinned players face systematically higher red-card risk after controlling for player characteristics, position, league, and exposure
the primary estimand is defined as the adjusted percentage-point change in P(red card) comparing dark-skinned (avg skin tone ≥0.5) to light-skinned (<0.5) players
the risk difference was estimated via marginal standardization (g-computation) using predictions from an adjusted logistic regression model
confidence intervals were computed via bootstrap with 2,000 iterations using the percentile method
adjusted P(red card | dark skin) = 1.402%
adjusted P(red card | light skin) = 1.218%
the risk difference is 0.184 percentage points
the 95% CI for the risk difference is [0.012, 0.355]
the two-sided p-value for the risk difference is 0.035
given the ~1.2% baseline risk, the risk difference represents about a 15% relative increase
the CI excludes zero, indicating statistical significance at α=0.05
the adjusted OR (dark vs light) is 1.157
the 95% CI for the OR is [1.016, 1.318]
the p-value for the OR is 0.028
dark-skinned players have 15.7% higher odds of a red card than light-skinned players after adjustment
the odds ratio is statistically significant since its CI excludes the null value of 1.0
the unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad, representing the interaction history between a specific player and referee across all matches
the original dataset had 146,028 dyads (2,053 players × 3,147 referees)
the final analytical sample had 115,603 dyads
dark-skinned dyads numbered 26,496 (22.9%)
light-skinned dyads numbered 89,107 (77.1%)
there were 1,455 red card events (1.26% overall rate)
there were 1,585 unique players
there were 2,978 unique referees
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator: any red card received
both direct red cards and second-yellow (yellow-red) cards were counted as red card events
the outcome was measured at the dyad level, aggregating across all encounters between a player and referee

spans.note: Exposure Variable / Skin tone classification labels

spans.assertion: skin tone was measured as the average of two independent raters' assessments from player profile photos
a 0 (very light) to 1 (very dark) scale was used, normalized from the original 1-5 scale
the inter-rater correlation was 0.923
exact rater agreement was 76.8%, and agreement within 0.25 units was 99.9%
dark skin was classified as average rating ≥0.5 and light skin as <0.5
this threshold was chosen as the midpoint between light and dark on the original 5-point scale
alternative skin-tone thresholds were tested in sensitivity analyses
the adjusted model controlled for a specified set of covariates to account for confounding
log-transformed number of games (median=1, mean=3.0) was included as a covariate to control for exposure/opportunity
player position (12 categories) was included as a covariate
position distribution differs by skin tone (dark-skinned players more likely forwards, less likely goalkeepers)
league country (4 categories) was included as a covariate to control for cross-national variation
standardized player age was included as a covariate (mean=27.1, SD=4.4)
standardized player height was included as a covariate (mean=182.2cm)
standardized player weight was included as a covariate (mean=76.4kg)
covariates were selected based on established associations with both skin tone and red-card risk, with games considered essential for exposure adjustment
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded for missing skin tone ratings (no profile photo)
8,461 dyads (5.8%) were excluded for missing player position
46 dyads (0.03%) were excluded for missing height
753 dyads (0.5%) were excluded for missing weight
a total of 30,425 dyads (20.8%) were excluded from the original sample
the final sample retained 115,603 dyads (79.2%)
the complete-case analysis assumes data are missing at random (MAR) conditional on observed covariates
players without profile photos may differ systematically from those with photos, potentially limiting generalizability of the skin-tone results
a logistic regression model with binary red-card outcome was specified
the model equation included skin_dark, log(games), position, league, age, height, and weight terms
maximum likelihood was used as the estimation method
Python 3.11 and statsmodels 0.14 were used as the software
the model successfully converged (maxiter=100)
model fit was Pseudo R²=0.095, AIC=14,182, BIC=14,375

the risk difference was computed via marginal standardization: fit the logistic model, create counterfactual datasets setting skin_dark to 1 and 0 for all dyads, predict P(red card) under both, average the predicted probabilities, and take their difference
OR confidence intervals were computed as Wald-type CIs from the logistic regression coefficient standard errors
risk-difference CIs were computed via non-parametric bootstrap (2,000 resamples), resampling at the dyad level with replacement, using the percentile method for the 95% CI
the bootstrap SE was 0.089 percentage points, with 1,999 of 2,000 iterations succeeding (99.95%)
the two-sided p-value was computed as twice the proportion of bootstrap resamples with sign opposite the point estimate, yielding p=0.035
a natural-log-based transformation was applied to the games variable (text truncated after 'Natural l...')

the analysis did not rule out alternative causal mechanisms — stereotype threat, opposing players provoking dark-skinned players more, or media/fan pressure on referees — as explanations for the association
the results are described as consistent with referee bias but not sufficient to definitively prove causation
experimental designs such as vignette studies of referee judgments would be needed to support causal claims, implying none were conducted
two estimands (risk difference and OR) were reported for the same hypothesis
multiple-testing concerns were judged minimal because both estimands were significant
sensitivity analyses across 3 thresholds were conducted
the sensitivity analyses were not formally adjusted for multiplicity
the primary model excluded referee country fixed effects due to convergence issues (157 countries, sparse data)
an alternative model including referee country FE showed a non-significant effect (OR=1.097, p=0.176)
this result was interpreted as possibly reflecting over-adjustment or loss of power from 157 parameters with only 1,455 events
country-level implicit/explicit bias measures (IAT, thermometer scores) were not included in the primary model, leaving referee-level characteristics not fully accounted for
two alternative skin-tone thresholds were tested to assess robustness of the binary classification
at threshold 0.375, adjusted OR=1.162 [1.031,1.310], p=0.014
at threshold 0.375, risk difference = 0.189pp
at threshold 0.375 the effect is significant and slightly stronger than the primary analysis
at threshold 0.5, adjusted OR=1.157 [1.016,1.318], p=0.028
at threshold 0.5, risk difference = 0.184pp
at threshold 0.5 the effect is significant, as reported in the primary analysis
at threshold 0.625, adjusted OR=1.094 [0.941,1.270], p=0.242
at threshold 0.625, risk difference = 0.112pp
at threshold 0.625 the effect is non-significant, though the point estimate remains positive
the effect is robust at thresholds 0.375 and 0.5 but becomes non-significant at 0.625
the effect is suggested to be driven mainly by the contrast between clearly light and somewhat-dark-or-darker players, with the restrictive threshold possibly lacking power due to smaller sample size
unadjusted red card rates by skin tone varied across the four leagues
Spain: dark 1.35%, light 1.63%, difference -0.28pp (unadjusted)
France: dark 1.32%, light 1.87%, difference -0.55pp (unadjusted)
England: dark 1.44%, light 1.11%, difference +0.33pp (unadjusted)
Germany: dark 1.22%, light 0.82%, difference +0.40pp (unadjusted)
the direction of the unadjusted effect varies by country: Germany and England show higher rates for dark-skinned players while Spain and France show the opposite
formal interaction testing would be needed to determine whether effect modification by league is significant, but this was not performed, and within-country sample sizes may be insufficient
red card rates vary substantially by position, with Center Backs highest (1.98%) and Attacking Midfielders lowest (0.71%)
within most positions dark-skinned players have slightly higher rates than light-skinned players, though the pattern is inconsistent (e.g. Goalkeepers reversed, possibly due to small sample)
position was included in the model as an important confounder
formal interaction testing for effect modification by position was not conducted, though no strong evidence of such modification was seen informally
the dataset includes country-level implicit bias (IAT) and explicit bias (racial thermometer) measures from Project Implicit
these bias measures were not included in the primary model
reason given: bias measures are constant within referee country, creating perfect collinearity with referee country fixed effects
reason given: country-level measures may not reflect individual referee biases
reason given: bias measures may post-date the 2012-2013 season
a future analysis could explore whether country-level bias moderates the skin tone effect, requiring interaction models; this was not done here
the analysis used dyad-level aggregation (total red cards across all encounters) rather than match-level analysis
match-level analysis would have advantages: accounting for within-dyad variation and allowing time-varying covariates
match-level analysis would have disadvantages: a much larger dataset (~373,000 observations), more complex modeling, and rarer events (0.5% per match)
dyad-level analysis was chosen for computational feasibility and interpretability, with the limitation that it averages over match-specific contexts
the reported effect is an average treatment effect (ATE) across all dyads that may vary by several factors
player prominence may moderate the effect (star vs bench players), untested
referee experience may moderate the effect, untested
match context (e.g. high-stakes matches) may moderate the effect, untested
heterogeneity analysis was not conducted due to lack of relevant variables and insufficient power for subgroup analyses
primary result: dark-skinned players face 0.184pp higher red-card risk than light-skinned players after adjustment (95% CI [0.012,0.355], p=0.035)
the effect represents a ~15% relative increase over the 1.2% baseline risk
the effect is statistically significant at α=0.05, with the 95% CI excluding zero
the effect is robust to thresholds 0.375 and 0.5 but not significant at the most restrictive threshold (0.625)
standard errors were not adjusted for clustering
additional limitations are noted: potential residual confounding, remaining missing-data concerns, and inability to definitively establish causality given the observational design
the hypothesis is concluded to be SUPPORTED
the data are interpreted as evidence consistent with systematic bias in red-card issuance favoring light-skinned over dark-skinned players in European professional soccer
all analyses were conducted in Python 3.11 using pandas 2.0.3, numpy 1.24.3, statsmodels 0.14.0, matplotlib 3.7.1, seaborn 0.12.2, and scipy 1.11.1
complete analysis code was provided in final_analysis.py, reproducing all results from data loading through final estimates
the random seed was set to 42 for bootstrap resampling
the data is available at /workspace/data/soccer/soccer.csv and the analysis can be fully reproduced by running the submitted script on it
